sec.title: Background
sec.p: Circadian biology suggests that synchronizing immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) dosing with morning peaks in immune activation could improve clinical outcomes, but well-powered studies using appropriate causal inference methodology are sparse.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We emulated a pragmatic randomized controlled trial of AM versus PM ICI infusions using Veterans Health Administration records from 2010 to 2024. In the emulated trial, stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer patients planned to undergo first-line or second-line ICI would have been randomized to receive the first three infusions in the AM (<12:00 PM) or PM (≥12:00 PM). The primary outcome was overall survival (OS). Marginal structural models with inverse probability of censoring weights estimated the per-protocol effect, accounting for baseline and longitudinal confounding. A historical chemotherapy cohort served as a negative control.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 4688 patients were eligible for the emulated trial; of these, 1171 received their first three infusions in the AM and 794 in the PM. Median follow-up was 4.7 years. Median survival was 10.3 months (AM) vs 8.1 months (PM). PM dosing was associated with worse OS (HR for PM versus AM 1.15, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.26, p=0.004). In 7951 chemotherapy controls (median follow-up 8.9 years), no time-of-day effect was detected (HR for PM vs AM 1.05, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.12, p=0.15). Results were robust in sensitivity analyses.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Morning ICI infusions confer a modest but clinically meaningful survival benefit that is absent in chemotherapy controls, supporting a causal chronotherapeutic effect. Scheduling ICIs before noon represents a low-cost, immediately actionable strategy warranting prospective confirmation.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Prior small, mostly retrospective studies suggest that administering immune checkpoint inhibitors earlier in the day might improve oncologic outcomes, but existing evidence has been limited by selection bias, time-varying confounding, immortal time bias, and lack of negative-control comparisons.

In a national Veterans Health Administration target trial emulation including 4688 patients with stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer receiving first-line or second-line immune checkpoint inhibitors, afternoon administration of the first three infusions was associated with worse overall survival than morning administration, while no comparable timing effect was observed in a chemotherapy negative control cohort.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE, OR POLICY

list-item.p: Scheduling immune checkpoint inhibitor infusions before noon is a low-cost strategy that warrants prospective randomized evaluation and could inform infusion-center scheduling policies if confirmed.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Administering immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) earlier in the day may enhance antitumor responses and improve survival. Circadian rhythms generate predictable morning peaks in immune activity, driving oscillations in immune cell trafficking into lymph nodes,1 tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density within the microenvironment,2 PD-1 expression,3 and suppressive myeloid populations.2 These findings support the “chronotherapy” hypothesis: aligning ICI administration with the immune system’s active phase could amplify therapeutic efficacy.4

A growing body of retrospective studies supports this hypothesis. Across multiple cancer types, early-day ICI administration has been consistently associated with longer progression-free and overall survival (OS).57 However, nearly all existing studies are non-randomized observational analyses with methodological limitations that preclude strong causal inference. Most are small, single-institution cohorts vulnerable to selection bias—for example, healthier patients may be more likely to receive morning infusions, while those with transportation challenges, rural residence, or multiple comorbidities may be scheduled in the afternoon. Time-varying confounding is common, as events like hospitalization during treatment can influence subsequent infusion timing. Many studies also suffer from immortal time bias, which arises when the exposure is defined after therapy initiation. Critically, none has included a negative-control comparator (eg, chemotherapy) to determine whether observed timing effects are specific to ICIs or reflect general prognostic differences.

The present study addresses these limitations by emulating a pragmatic target randomized trial within the national Veterans Health Administration (VHA). Using the largest-to-date cohort of stage IV non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients treated with ICIs, we apply a marginal structural model that accounts for time-varying treatment strategies, eliminates immortal-time bias, and balances both baseline and longitudinal confounding through inverse-probability weighting. A contemporaneous cohort of chemotherapy-treated patients serves as a negative control to test residual confounding unrelated to immune mechanisms. Our objective was to build on emerging randomized evidence8 by providing a comprehensive and methodologically rigorous observational evaluation of ICI chronotherapy.

sec.title: Emulated trial protocol
sec.p: We designed a pragmatic randomized trial comparing morning versus afternoon ICI infusions and emulated this target trial using observational data from VHA. The hypothetical trial would have enrolled all patients with stage IV NSCLC scheduled to initiate ICI therapy in the first or second line, without exclusions based on performance status or organ function. This inclusive design is justified by the possibility that all patients undergoing ICI therapy could benefit from optimized infusion timing if it improves survival or response, given the low-risk nature of the scheduling intervention.

In the target trial, patients would be enrolled and randomized at the time a plan for ICI therapy was formulated; in our emulation, this was approximated as the date ICI therapy was ordered in the electronic health record. Patients would be randomized to receive their first three ICI infusions either entirely in the morning (before 12 PM) or entirely in the afternoon (after 12 PM). Protocol deviations were defined as receiving one or more of the first three infusions outside the assigned time window, or failure to receive at least one infusion within 30 days of the ICI order. However, patients who received only one or two infusions in total were not considered to have deviated from protocol, provided those infusions were consistent with the assigned timing arm. After the third infusion, patients could schedule subsequent treatments at their discretion. We focused on the first three infusions based on prior studies suggesting that this early period may be critical for priming antitumor immunity.811

Patients were followed according to usual care, and OS (the primary outcome) was assessed using administrative data. We applied the same emulated trial protocol to a chemotherapy-treated control cohort, using the date of chemotherapy order as the proxy for enrollment and randomization, and otherwise mirroring eligibility criteria, exposure assignment, and outcome ascertainment.

sec.title: Data source and study cohorts
sec.p: This study used electronic medical record data from the VHA Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW), which includes data for all Veterans receiving care through VHA facilities nationwide.

For the primary ICI-treated cohort, we identified all patients from 2015 to 2024 with metastatic NSCLC in the national VHA system with at least one order for an ICI with FDA approval (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, or atezolizumab) and who were treated with ICI in the first or second line. Stage and cancer histology were ascertained through VA Cancer Registry System data. Line of therapy was identified through CPT codes for systemic therapy infusions as previously described.12 For the chemotherapy control cohort, we identified all metastatic NSCLC patients with an order for common chemotherapeutics (cisplatin, carboplatin, paclitaxel, pemetrexed, gemcitabine, etoposide, or docetaxel) in the first or second line from 2010 to 2024 (extending the date window to 2010 to include patients treated before initial NSCLC ICI approval in 2015).

sec.title: Infusion times
sec.p: Accurately determining the true time of immunotherapy infusion is challenging in large-scale, heterogeneous electronic medical record data. Although the scheduled encounter time is often available in structured fields, it is an unreliable proxy for actual infusion time due to patient arrival variability, administration of pre-medications, and sequencing of co-administered drugs, particularly in chemo-immunotherapy regimens where cytotoxic agents may be infused before ICIs. To address this, we leveraged prior work developing a method to identify structured nursing infusion documentation, in which infusion nurses record the exact start and stop times of each drug administration.13 14 While formatting varies by site, this documentation is reliably present across VHA facilities that administer infusion therapies, though not all sites consistently recorded time-stamped data throughout the study period. We extracted all available infusion documentation and used an open-source large language model (Meta Llama 3.3 70B) to identify the exact ICI infusion initiation time for each encounter. In the chemotherapy control group, we similarly extracted the time of the first chemotherapeutic drug administered. This algorithm was over 97% accurate in determining AM versus PM infusion times (additional details are presented in the online supplemental Methods).

sec.title: Covariates
sec.p: We collected comprehensive baseline data on a range of factors that could influence whether patients received morning versus afternoon ICI infusions. Patient-level variables included age, sex, self-reported race, marital status, employment status, geographic region, Area Deprivation Index (ADI), Rural/Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) designation, distance from the patient’s residence to their primary VA facility, smoking status, body mass index, Charlson Comorbidity Index, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, and healthcare utilization in the prior year, including emergency department visits, social work encounters, and mental health visits. Cancer-related variables included tumor histology and PD-L1 expression. Treatment-related factors included the planned ICI regimen (monotherapy vs combination with chemotherapy), the time from diagnosis to the ICI order date, and the number of prior lines of systemic therapy (0 or 1). To account for changes in clinical status during the exposure period, we also included inpatient versus outpatient status as a time-varying longitudinal covariate, capturing hospitalizations that may influence infusion timing between enrollment and the third infusion.

Demographic information, comorbidities, and healthcare utilization were extracted from the VA CDW. ADI, RUCA designation, and the distance from the patient’s residence to their primary VA facility were calculated using geocoded residential address data. PD-L1 expression was extracted using a validated natural language processing algorithm.15 ECOG performance status was identified using regular expressions applied to Hematology/Oncology provider notes.16 Tumor histology was obtained from the VA Cancer Registry System.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: We used a marginal structural modeling approach (clone-censor-weight (CCW)) to emulate the target trial, following established methodology.1719 The CCW method addresses both baseline and time-varying confounding, allows proper alignment of time zero with the ICI order date (rather than treatment initiation) reflecting the time of enrollment and randomization in the target trial, and ensures treatment arms are balanced over the course of therapy. Details of the CCW method and our implementation are presented in the online supplemental Methods. Following the CCW procedure, we estimated the effect of PM (vs AM) infusion timing on OS using weighted Cox proportional hazards regression. We used the weighted Kaplan-Meier estimator to compare median survival and survival probabilities at 6, 12, and 24 months. SEs and 95% CIs were computed using robust variance estimators.

Median follow-up time in each cohort was calculated using the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. For descriptive summaries, patients were categorized based on the actual timing of their first three ICI infusions as AM, PM, or mixed. All analyses were performed using R V.4.4.1. The data cut-off for the analysis was August 19, 2024. Missing data handling is described in the online supplemental Methods. Sensitivity analyses varied the infusion time cut-off defining AM versus PM infusions, implemented a landmark analysis to test sensitivity to our analytic method, and explored how the required number of consistent AM or PM infusions (3 in the main text; varied from 1 to 4 in sensitivity analyses) affected our results. These are described in the online supplemental Methods.

sec.title: Cohort characteristics
sec.p: We identified 4688 patients planned for ICI therapy who would have been eligible for our target trial (online supplemental figure 1 for patient selection diagram). Their characteristics are shown in table 1, grouped according to the subsequent ICI infusion times they actually received. Baseline covariates were overall similar among patients who received the first three infusions all in the AM versus PM, though PM patients tended to be slightly older (58% over 70 years old vs 53%), be retired (36% vs 33%), live in isolated small rural towns (5.0% vs 2.6%), live over 50 miles from their primary VA facility (23% vs 14.2%), have ECOG 2 or higher performance status (38.4% vs 28.0%), have a social work visit in the prior year (44% vs 32%), and be treated with ICI monotherapy rather than combination with chemotherapy (60% monotherapy vs 48%). Patients who received mixed AM and PM infusions tended to have intermediate covariate values between the AM and PM groups. Patients who did not receive any treatment within the 30-day grace period tended to have poorer performance status and higher rates of unknown PD-L1 status. Median follow-up was 4.7 years. The median infusion time was 11:45 AM (IQR 10:45 AM to 1:00 PM); only 3.2% of infusions occurred after 3 PM.

sec.p: The chemotherapy control cohort included 7951 patients (online supplemental Table 1). The AM and PM groups showed similar differences as the ICI group, with PM patients having slightly worse performance status, higher comorbidities, and more rural and distant residences. Median follow-up was 8.9 years. The median infusion time was 11:48 AM (IQR 10:50 AM to 12:55 PM); 2.5% of infusions occurred after 3 PM.

sec.title: Primary analysis
sec.p: Both ICI and chemotherapy cohorts were well balanced in terms of baseline covariates after applying the CCW procedure (balance statistics can be found in online supplemental figures 2 and 3). In the primary analysis for the ICI cohort, median survival was 10.3 months in the AM arm and 8.11 months in the PM arms (figure 1). PM infusions were associated with worse OS (adjusted HR (aHR) 1.15, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.26, p=0.004; table 2). At 12 months, the estimated absolute decrement in survival probability in the PM arm was −5.9% (95% CI −1.2% to −10.6%). In the chemotherapy cohort, we observed survival decrement with PM infusions (aHR 1.05, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.12, p=0.15; figure 1). Median survival in the chemotherapy cohort was 7.9 months in the AM arm and 7.2 months in the PM arm.

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: Altering the time cut-off to 11 AM instead of 12 PM did not substantially change the results in either cohort (figure 2a and table 2; see online supplemental figure 4 for Kaplan-Meier curves). Estimation uncertainty increased at the 1 PM time cut-off, especially in the immunotherapy cohort, with wider CIs and a more uncertain effect. In the landmark analyses varying the number of infusions required in the AM or PM in each arm (from 1 to 4), the effect of AM infusions on OS was negligible with the first infusion but became apparent at the second and third infusion (figure 2b). At the fourth infusion, uncertainty increased due to the small number of patients who received all four infusions in the AM or PM. For the chemotherapy group, the landmark analyses showed no effect of infusion timing on OS in any of the analyses (figure 2). Kaplan-Meier plots for each landmark analysis are provided in online supplemental figure 5.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this retrospective cohort study using national VHA data and robust causal inference methods, we found that receiving the first three ICI infusions before noon was associated with a modest but clinically meaningful improvement in OS among patients with stage IV NSCLC. This survival benefit was not observed in a chemotherapy-treated negative control group, supporting a time-of-day-specific effect linked to ICI biology rather than non-specific prognostic differences. The effect emerged after the second infusion and remained consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses, including alternative time-of-day cutoffs. These findings suggest that rescheduling ICI infusions to the morning may be a low-cost, low-risk strategy to improve outcomes that warrants evaluation in prospective randomized trials.

Our results align with a growing body of literature suggesting that earlier ICI administration improves survival. Following the landmark study by Qian et al,5 which reported nearly a doubling of OS in melanoma patients who received fewer than 20% of infusions after 4:30 PM, subsequent studies have confirmed this effect, extended it to other cancers including NSCLC, and explored optimal time cutoffs and dosing windows.20 However, prior studies have been limited by small sample sizes and major methodological shortcomings. None, to our knowledge, have fully addressed the time-dependent nature of infusion timing, including longitudinal confounding (eg, hospitalizations), immortal time bias, and duration bias (patients who live longer are more likely to receive a mix of AM and PM infusions by chance, biasing the sample of patients who received only AM or only PM infusions). Prior studies also lacked adequate control for key baseline confounders such as performance status, rurality, and travel distance. Critically, none incorporated a negative control group to assess whether observed timing effects were specific to ICIs.

Our study addresses these key limitations of the prior literature and provides stronger evidence for a causal relationship between ICI infusion timing and survival. By applying a marginal structural modeling approach, we appropriately account for the time-dependent nature of the exposure and adjust for longitudinal confounding. We also incorporate extensive controls for baseline factors that may influence assignment to AM versus PM infusion slots, substantially expand the sample size, and evaluate the robustness of the observed effect using a chemotherapy-treated negative control group. Together, these methodological improvements yield what we believe is a more realistic estimate of the true effect size—an OS HR of approximately 0.87 for morning versus afternoon infusions, compared with the ~0.50 estimates reported in earlier studies. This more conservative effect size is critical for informing power calculations and the design of future randomized controlled trials, as underpowered studies risk missing a genuine, but modest, survival benefit.

The first randomized trial investigating the impact of ICI infusion timing was recently reported.21 This study enrolled 210 patients with advanced NSCLC receiving combination chemoimmunotherapy and randomized them to receive their first four infusions either before or after 3 PM. Patients in the morning arm had significantly higher objective response rates as well as improved progression-free and OS. While these findings suggest a larger effect size than observed in our study, their generalizability may be limited. Very few ICI infusions in the VHA—fewer than 4%—occur after 3 PM. The vast majority take place between 10 AM and 3 PM, meaning that the randomized trial’s time cut-off captures a much more extreme contrast than would be typical in real-world practice in the VHA or similar health systems. Our use of a 12 PM cut-off likely reflects a more realistic and actionable comparison, though it may result in a more modest effect size. These considerations highlight the need for additional randomized trials using more practical time cut-offs and larger sample sizes. Given the low-risk nature of infusion scheduling as an intervention, this question is well-suited for a pragmatic, decentralized trial design within integrated health systems such as the VHA.

Our study has several limitations. First, although we applied state-of-the-art causal inference methods and adjusted for a wide range of confounders, the possibility of residual unmeasured confounding cannot be excluded. Second, the range of infusion times within the VHA was relatively narrow, typically between 10 AM and 3 PM. If infusions administered later in the afternoon or evening have a more pronounced negative impact on outcomes (as suggested above), our study may underestimate the true effect of infusion timing. Third, the chemotherapy control group primarily included patients receiving first-line treatment, whereas the ICI group comprised both first-line and second-line patients. Chemotherapy patients were also slightly younger and healthier on average. While these differences are unlikely to substantially bias our findings, it is possible that younger, healthier patients were more able to attend early appointments, introducing additional confounding in the chemotherapy group. Fourth, the VHA population is predominantly male, which may limit the generalizability of our findings to female patients; chemotherapy chronomodulation has been reported to be more effective in males.22 Fifth, while we focused on OS—a critically important clinical endpoint—we did not assess radiographic progression, given the challenges of extracting reliable progression data from structured records at this scale. Finally, we were unable to evaluate immune-related adverse events, which are difficult to reliably identify in structured data but may be more frequent with morning ICI dosing if immune activation is heightened.

In summary, we suggest that morning ICI infusions are associated with a small but significant improvement in OS compared with afternoon infusions. These data can inform subsequent randomized trials and could represent a low-cost, scalable means to improve patient survival.
